You’re not broken. You’re cyclical.

We’ve been conditioned to expect the same energy, focus, and output from ourselves every single day. But that standard was built on research that largely excluded women — and it shows.

Women have two biological clocks. The circadian rhythm (24 hours) and the infradian rhythm (28 days). The second one governs your hormones, metabolism, immune function, and stress response across your entire cycle.

Cycle syncing isn’t a wellness trend. It’s pattern recognition. It’s learning to work with your biology instead of spending your energy fighting it.

Swipe through to understand what it actually is, what it isn’t, and why this is the framework everything else builds on here.

posts.bodyHtml:
I. The name we lived with — and what it got wrong

What’s wild about this syndrome is that it is nearly impossible to pinpoint when it all started. There are suggestions that the syndrome was referred to as early as Hippocrates (460-377 BC) in medical notes (unreal). A description of PCOS popped up again in 1791 when an Italian scientist described a married, infertile woman with shiny ovaries with a white surface that appeared the size of pigeon eggs.

Fast forward to 1935 (yes, that long- sigh). The modern history of PCOS truly begins (we have had a lot of “starts” here) with a pivotal paper by Stein and Leventhal investigating polycystic ovary syndrome. Essentially, they saw what looked like “little sacs” on a patient’s ovaries and thought they might be cysts of some kind. She also had high levels of male hormones and couldn’t get pregnant. Because of this, they called it polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

While this seemed to make sense at the time, doctors didn’t know that these were just symptoms of a much broader endocrine and metabolic disorder that affects the whole body. These “cysts” are actually fluid-filled sacs that have immature eggs, and now, you don’t even have to have these “cysts” to have or be diagnosed with PCOS. This led to widespread patient confusion, and a lack of diagnoses.

II. The harm wasn't abstract, it was systemic

The problem is that the idea of “cysts” continued to get in the way of the true nature of the disease. This terminology led to significant diagnostic delays affecting up to 70% of those with the condition, as well as fragmented care. Because the name pointed solely to the ovaries and fertility, many women weren’t diagnosed unless they presented the “classic” picture - cysts plus fertility struggles. Women would go to numerous specialists to treat individual symptoms, but never addressed the full picture. Without a proper diagnosis, patients are essentially playing whack-a-mole with symptoms as they crop up.

III. What PMOS actually means & the science behind the name

After a decade of debate, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) has now become polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), thanks to a global panel of clinicians, researchers, and patient advocates that recently published a paper in the Lancet.

The change follows an extensive international consensus process (more than 14,000 survey responses from patients and healthcare professionals from around the world). The new terminology is intended to “improve diagnostic clarity, reduce stigma, strengthen research consistency, and better align treatment strategies with the underlying biology of the disease”. The investigators wrote “accuracy was improved by omitting cysts and by capturing endocrine, metabolic, and ovarian dysfunction”.

The paper, “Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, the new name for polycystic ovary syndrome: a multistep global consensus process” (wordy title, great paper) explains how the syndrome can cause disturbances in insulin signaling, androgen production, neuroendocrine pathways, and ovarian function. The disturbances and abnormalities “contribute to not only infertility and menstrual dysfunction, but also to obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease risk, mental health conditions, and pregnancy complications”. In short, yes, it is a full-body disease, folks.

IV. Why this name change is bigger than semantics

So, what will this even do? I mean we took ten years to change the name- why?

We’ve covered this a bit but let’s get this list going. Good things that can come from this:

  • This will hopefully lead to faster and more accurate diagnoses for women

  • It will improve awareness of the syndrome

  • It will expand treatment options beyond fertility management alone (metabolic treatments, endocrine treatments, etc.)

  • This may also open the door for future research to refine PMOS subtypes and enable more personalized therapeutic strategies

  • It will provide a clearer framework for understanding the condition’s complexity (and longer-term health implications)

  • This will hopefully allow for more research and funding (which we clearly and desperately need)

V. What this means for women who have it

Making this name change, and spreading awareness should help current patient populations. While this doesn’t cure the condition, it does make treatment options broader and easier to access. It should hopefully allow you to be heard, understood, and listened to.

Also, for the record, it should make you feel frickin’ validated. This is NOT just a reproductive disease, you are NOT alone, and this is NOT your fault.

VI. The bigger pattern

This is all part of a longer story about women’s health being dismissed, minimized, or misnamed. It is frustrating that it took a decade to rename something we’ve long understood to be an endocrine and metabolic syndrome.

However, getting more attention and research on PMOS is, in itself, groundbreaking.

I’m going to leave us on a note from an amazing woman, Lorna Berry, an Australian woman who has PMOS and played a key role in the renaming process.

“This is about accountability and progress,” she said. “It is about my daughters, their daughters, and the countless women yet to be born. We deserve clarity, understanding, and equitable healthcare from the very beginning.”

Couldn’t have said it better myself.

Train through it. Recover from it. Thrive beyond it.

Madeleine

posts.bodyHtml:
Three years ago I had never even heard the term “pelvic floor”. Many of us haven’t, and by the time we do hear about it, it is because we have an issue with it. I’ve learned (as you will, too) that the pelvic floor is incredibly important and pelvic floor PT might just be the exact thing you need.

What is the Pelvic Floor, Actually?

What the heck actually is it? Good news for you- I have a great definition and an even better diagram below (kidding on the diagram). The pelvic floor is a group of muscles, ligaments, and connective tissues that form a hammock-like base across the bottom of the pelvis. It supports the bladder, uterus, and rectum, controls continence, and plays a role in sexual function, core stability, and intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) management. This “hammock” of muscles does a LOT- no wonder that if things go awry it can cause so many issues.

The Two Types of Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

There are two types of pelvic floor dysfunction and they both require different types of treatment. Let’s go over both types:

  • Hypotonic (the one everyone talks about- think someone in your life trying kegels)

    • Hypotonic refers to weakness and under-activity

    • Common after childbirth and in older women

    • Symptoms: leaking when you sneeze, prolapse, general weakness

    • Treatment: Kegels, biofeedback, progressive loading/functional movement

  • Hypertonic (lesser known but equally important)

    • Hypertonic refers to tightness and overactivity (the pelvic floor can’t fully relax)

    • Strongly associated with endometriosis, chronic pelvic pain, stress, trauma

    • Symptoms: pain with penetration, pain during workouts, tightness, incomplete bladder emptying, pelvic pressure

    • Treatment: release work, diaphragmatic breathing, manual therapy, progressive relaxation

What Pelvic Floor PT Looks Like

Pelvic floor PT sounds like a weird thing to sign up for. As someone who has gone through it, let me demystify a bit.

First off - it isn’t scary or weird (ok, I guess at first it is a little weird). Your first appointment will more than likely be more of a diagnostic appointment. You will tell them what is happening, give history, and they might do an external and internal exam.

The external exam may go over breathing technique, your spine, hips, legs, and feet, as well as core stability (yes, this plays a big role in your pelvic floor), balance, and movement patterns. The therapist may ask you to perform certain movements to reveal muscle imbalances, weakness, or other issues. They may also press areas around the groin, inner thighs, and abdomen to assess the pelvic floor and surrounding muscles.

The internal part might require a bit of a pelvic exam to get the lay of the land. Yes, this means they will glove up, and use their fingers inside of your vaginal canal to feel the muscles. I know this sounds absolutely bizarre, but let’s keep in mind that this pelvic floor PT does this every day and sees tons of patients. They are trained professionals, after all. Also, once you do it once, it gets way less weird.

All other appointments will be comprised of exercises, education, and/or internal work. You will have a private room (duh) and depending on your condition, you may have exercises to do at home.

Finding the Right Pelvic Floor PT

It is important to find someone who you’re comfortable with and that you trust. By the time I was done with my pelvic floor PT, I was not remotely phased by someone doing internal work (shout out to Sarah, my pelvic floor PT, who made my experience lovely). As someone who has been there, done that, I’m telling you that you can absolutely handle it and will be so happy you did it.

If possible, ask around to friends and doctors to see if they recommend anyone. There are usually more women than you think that have gone themselves or know a good pelvic floor PT. Additionally, if possible, try to find someone who takes your insurance. Due to the hands-on nature, and privacy required for these types of appointments, there can sometimes be an additional fee (which makes it more expensive than traditional PT). While you’re looking around and finding the right ones, confirm that your pelvic floor PT has experience in the condition that you have (for example, my pelvic floor PT knew a LOT about endo and worked closely with my surgeon- she was highly recommended for my condition).

Who is This For?

Everyone. I firmly believe that pelvic floor therapy is for everyone. You don’t have to have an underlying condition to go and learn more about this essential muscle group. If you are in pain or have an underlying condition, pelvic floor PT seems almost non-negotiable. Understanding where pain is stemming from and how to improve it can greatly improve your quality of life. Consider this my official endorsement for you to go and try this. You will thank yourself.

As always, reach out with questions-EveryWoman is always here to talk about it.

Train through it. Recover from it. Thrive beyond it.

Madeleine

Johns Hopkins Medicine. (n.d.). Pelvic floor therapy. Johns Hopkins Medicine. https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/treatment-tests-and-therapies/pelvic-floor-therapy

posts.bodyHtml:
Why You Even Have to Fight

It is disheartening to even have to write the “why” here, but it is deeply important. According to a systemic literature review (source cited below), an endometriosis diagnosis can face delays of up to ten years. Some papers say it can range from 0.3 to 12 years. Sadly, PCOS diagnoses also face delays. The WHO says that it takes more than 2 years on average and up to 3+ healthcare providers to get a diagnosis. Even after all of that, they suspect up to 70% of PCOS cases go undiagnosed.

These stats are rough, but they are getting better. In my opinion, it is better to know what you’re up against in this journey. This process will require you to advocate for yourself, and to push back. Let’s get into how best to do this.

Know Your Symptoms

Knowing your symptoms is key. Track symptoms over your cycle. Write everything down in your notes app, in a journal, in a period or symptom tracker. Having this data over a few cycles will help make your case. It will also be helpful for you to notice trends in your body, and help you best know how to predict how you might be feeling.

In parallel, write down EVERY weird thing you remember from your past. Were your periods always bad? Have any weird symptoms developed? Have you always felt like this or did this come on recently? These things may seem trivial, but they add up. For example, I never had bad periods. However, I had severe migraines with aura that came on when I was 21 that caused me to violently vomit for hours on end, I had fatigue, chronic infections, random pelvic pain, etc. All of these things together painted a picture, but siloed, they never added up. Make sure you tell your doctor ALL symptoms, even if they seem weird or unrelated.

How To Talk To Your Doctor

When talking to your doctor, language matters. Instead of saying “oh sometimes my periods hurt really bad”, you have to really explain what you mean. Replace that with a statement like “I have intense cyclical pelvic pain that leaves me doubled over when I’m on my period”. Show them your documentation and data that you’ve tracked. Tell them your history in a linear and straightforward way.

Ask as many questions as you want. Bring up endometriosis and PCOS. Tell them you’ve done research and that you want help finding out what is going on. You have permission to push back, and you have permission to be difficult if your message isn’t getting through.

Building Your Case Like a File

I want to do a deeper dive into this topic later, but building your own medical file and history is SO helpful in the long term. Ask for copies of EVERYTHING. Write down notes. Save pdfs from your doctor’s portal into a folder on your computer. Save photos from surgeries, ultrasounds, etc. A lot of doctors and hospital systems use different online portal providers and things can get messy and unorganized quickly. It is powerful to show up with your own medical file that tracks and shows your history. It gives doctors a full picture, and you will save countless hours.

Another suggestion is to ask to record the appointments you have (just use your phone to do so). This advice was given to me and was a lifesaver when I first met an endo specialist. I felt like I was on information overload and those appointments can be highly emotional. Being able to play back what your doctor said when you are in a calmer headspace is invaluable.

When They Don’t Believe You

I’ve said it once already, but I’m going to say it again. If you’re not being heard or listened to, you can be difficult. You have permission to tell your doctor that they’re not listening to you. You also have permission to walk out and find a new one. I actually highly recommend this course of action if you’re being told that the pain is normal or to just take some Tylenol (yes, this phrase AGAIN- I will never not be angry at this). If your gut is telling you something is wrong, trust it. Worst case scenario, you see a few doctors and it really is nothing. You have every right to be heard, to be treated with respect, and to advocate for yourself.

Final Thoughts

I will admit that a lot of these steps aren’t super fun or easy. However, one could argue that there is a lot in life that isn’t fun or easy (just add all of this to the list right next to “go to the dentist”). Having a plan before you go in, tracking your symptoms, and keeping copies of your records will arm you best for appointments with doctors. You can find providers who will listen, work with you, and give your symptoms the attention they deserve.

Send this to someone who is struggling to get a diagnosis. Tell them to reach out to me and I can give more advice- that is what EveryWoman is for.

Train through it. Recover from it. Thrive beyond it.

Madeleine

P.S. - I thought of my friend Emily M. when I wrote the “When They Don’t Believe You” section- she is a fellow “difficult woman” whom I adore; this one is for you.

posts.bodyHtml:
What's Actually Happening in Your Body

Polycystic ovary syndrome has a misleading name (great, let’s add more complexity here!). At a very basic level, it is a common condition that affects women’s hormones and has many different underlying symptoms. Essentially, a patient with PCOS has ovaries that create excess androgens (this is another group of hormones that includes testosterone), which causes your reproductive hormones to become imbalanced. Women who have PCOS may have small follicle cysts on their ovaries (hence, the name). These cysts are fluid-filled sacs that have immature eggs.

Because of this imbalance of hormones, the body shows a lot of different symptoms. Some people say that it is “just irregular periods”, but that is far from the case. This syndrome affects the entire body.

Doctors and researchers do not know the cause of PCOS. Some leading theories include insulin resistance, low-grade inflammation, hereditary links, and excess androgen. Many of these potential causes are actually also potential consequences of PCOS (so this quickly becomes a chicken or the egg situation).

Symptoms - The Full Picture

PCOS is a syndrome. This means that it presents in every woman’s body differently. Here are some of the common listed symptoms (a far from comprehensive list):

  • Irregular periods

  • Abnormal hair growth

  • Acne

  • Weight gain/obesity

  • Darkening of the skin

  • Cysts on the ovaries

  • Skin tags

  • Thinning hair

  • Infertility

  • Insulin Resistance

Getting Diagnosed (And Why It's Often Delayed)

Getting diagnosed with PCOS involves using the Rotterdam criteria (established in 2003). As of now, the medical community says that you need to have two out of the three criteria to be diagnosed:

  1. Irregular periods or absent ovulation

  2. Clinical or biochemical signs of excess androgen

  3. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound

Additionally, it is worth noting that a lot of other conditions have to be ruled out before making a diagnosis (the Rotterdam criteria aren’t applied in isolation).

Given that you only need two out of three for diagnosis (which allows the syndrome to be presented in many different ways), and that you have to rule out a lot of other conditions, getting an official PCOS diagnosis can be challenging and take many years.

What This Means for Movement

Research shows that strength training is incredibly beneficial if you have PCOS. Resistance training lowers insulin resistance, directly improving PCOS symptoms. It also has a longer post-exercise metabolic effect (so glucose clearing extends after the workout itself).

However, although counterproductive, doing endless amounts of cardio to lose weight or feel better often backfires. Think back-to-back HIIT sessions or daily long runs only. This increases cortisol and inflammation, making PCOS worse.

The idea here is to improve and manage symptoms. This is not to say that you can’t ever do HIIT again or run a marathon (if this is your dream, you can still make this happen). It is knowing what movement can do for you, and how to best utilize it to help you feel better. It might also include some trial and error until you learn what works best for you.

Lifestyle as Lever (Not a Moral Obligation)

There are lifestyle changes that you can make that might help mitigate symptoms. Again, everyone is different, and not all options help every single person in the right way. Think of these things as a lever (and as the title of this section reads, not a moral obligation- we are so over that way of thinking). The research isn’t extensive, but we’ve got some to go on.

A few things that we do know:

  • Starving yourself is NOT the answer. To be fair, this never is the answer for really anything, but especially PCOS. If you starve yourself you will spike cortisol (bad), trigger insulin spikes (bad), and you will lose muscle instead of fat (really bad). Research shows that women who eat higher amounts of protein (along with healthy fats and moderate carbohydrates) have higher success rates of stopping blood sugar spikes and feeling better.

  • Poor sleep often makes PCOS worse. Again, this is almost never great so don’t think you’re special on this one.

  • Chronic stress exacerbates PCOS. I personally HATE when people say this one. When has a doctor telling you to lower your stress ever helped or actually lowered your stress? Never. I hate hearing this (life is so stressful all the time?), but I do think there are some things that you can implement that help it a little bit.

  • Not recovering from training can cause more cortisol to be produced and can hurt the hormonal picture rather than help it. Ensuring you have ample time for recovery is incredibly important.

There are some others that doctors mention that I hesitated to state (but ultimately decided to include with caveats). Some doctors say losing weight is beneficial. I personally find this incredibly nuanced, oftentimes unrealistic, and honestly, sometimes insulting. Additionally, most doctors say to avoid alcohol (this is a personal choice and I don’t think me opining on how many glasses of wine you should have a week is productive here).

Where I Leave You (For Now)

You may have already known everything listed in this post or you may have learned about a new diagnosis you had no idea about. It is an exciting time in PCOS and PCOS research: many clinicians are excited about using Metformin and GLP-1s as potential treatments for patients, we have more data about PCOS and fertility, and we have more research coming out about how to use lifestyle changes to help women feel better. PCOS sucks, let’s not downplay that. But we have tools in our toolkit and that makes things feel more hopeful. Send this on to someone who might need to read it.

Train through it. Recover from it. Thrive beyond it.

Madeleine

posts.bodyHtml:
Most of 2023 had me feeling like I was racking up frequent flyer miles at the hospital. First came an emergency appendectomy in the Spring. Then Fall arrived, and with it, excision surgery. Two days later, I found myself back in the ER with a severe kidney infection (that I was hospitalized overnight for). I was bedridden, I couldn’t move, and I couldn’t eat. This is not an inspirational comeback story where I miraculously bounced back by sheer force of will - it is a story that started in a hospital bed.

When Rest Is Not A Choice

The days and weeks after surgery and my subsequent hospitalization felt hard. It was surrendering to total rest. Not the glamorous rest with candles, herbal tea, bubble baths, etc. It was not being able to get up and use the bathroom by myself. It was sleeping for long periods, trying to stay hydrated, and watching a lot of really bad reality tv (which, I will admit is a guilty pleasure, so not a total loss here). The emotional weight of being someone who loves to move and not being able to and the loss of independence felt crushing. However, it became clear that rest was not a choice. It became a necessity to help my body heal, recover, and try its best to stabilize.

These Boots Are Made For Walking

My shift back to movement started with walking. Short walks that were really slow. Walks that hurt my back because I couldn’t engage my core (this is from all the incisions and the way that the doctors have to inflate your abdomen to get visibility during surgery). Implementing these walks felt like such a win. They helped me get out of the house. They allowed me to get fresh air and see the sun. They gave me a sense of independence that I felt like I was lacking. They helped my mental health in ways that made such a difference. You don’t realize what a privilege walking is until you lose the ability to do so.

Building From The Ground Up

Thus began the slow, unglamorous reality of recovery. I lacked core muscles, was losing muscle density, and still had incisions that were healing.

I walked every day until I built up strength. After 6 weeks, I began pelvic floor PT to build back strength in my pelvic region. We worked on breaking up scar tissue on my stomach (which is decidedly unpleasant but necessary and worth it), and I learned how to connect with muscles I didn’t even know I had. There were still things I couldn’t do, but I worked around them.

I then began slowly getting back in the pool for short swims. I worked on stretching and building back up mobility. I tried to be present in my body and feel when things felt good, when they hurt, and when I needed to slow down. The process had a lot of setbacks and a lot of frustration, but with time, things came back.

The Road Back to the Weight Room

As a lifelong athlete, I was no stranger to lifting weights. However, after getting diagnosed, I did a massive deep dive on women’s health. I read a copious number of books, listened to podcasts, read articles, and talked to doctors about what was recommended, what studies had been done, and what the data showed.

It became clear that the one thing that almost everyone agreed on (a rarity) was resistance training. It was time to get strong, not only to help with endometriosis, but for longevity, bone density, brain health, etc. I hired a trainer and began focusing on what real resistance training, correct programming, and good form looked like. I learned that my body was resilient and that gaining strength helped me in almost every aspect of my life.

What I Know Now That I Didn’t Know Then

There are so many things I wish I could tell myself back then. Patience (which is admittedly not my strong suit) ended up playing more of a role in this than anything else. Using rest, proper nutrition, and building a team of care professionals that helped me through my healing journey was paramount.

In the mainstream fitness world, there is no roadmap in place for women recovering from excision surgery. Every woman deserves a plan that works for their body and that is what EveryWoman exists to do.

If you’re recovering from surgery and don’t know where to start, reach out.

Train through it. Recover from it. Thrive beyond it.

Madeleine

posts.bodyHtml:
I recently heard the quote “You are the CEO of your own life” on a podcast while walking the dog. When I heard this, I thought- yes! Then I got home and thought, actually, wait: most women are the CEOs of multiple people’s lives (and for that matter homes, families, etc.) Then, after even further thought, I came to the conclusion that being a CEO is exhausting and actually, this is an unpaid position and I don’t think I want this job?

The good news is, we can take the “CEO” title, and apply it to things in our life that matter to us. We can use this title to pursue things that can help us have a better quality of life, bring joy and peace, and make us feel better. It is good news that you are in control of your health. It is a good thing that you are in charge of picking your care, doctors, treatments, etc. because you know you best.

Every single woman will need a care team throughout their life. Humans are complex- we have different needs, different issues, and our medical care needs to reflect that. Let’s talk about building a team that works for you.

The System is Not Built For Complex Conditions (or Women in General)

The US healthcare system is not built to treat a “whole person” (sigh, I have many thoughts about the US healthcare system, but I will not get into this in this article). The medical system is segmented and is incredibly reactive not proactive. This systemic design leaves a lot of gaps, as many chronic conditions affect the whole body.

Women have an even harder go of it - in 2020 only 5% of global research and development funding went towards women’s health. In a surprise to essentially no-one in this country, in FY2024 only 10% of the NIH’s congressional appropriation went towards women’s health. Oh, and did I mention that chronic illness affects women at higher rates, too? [Ugh, now that I’m writing this, the staggering statistics and utter lack of funding for women and their health will also be another article I publish.]

I’m hoping the system changes (and have faith that it will one day). In the meantime, we must operate within this system and advocate for ourselves (and others) wherever and whenever possible. The intermediate path forward is creating a team of care providers that work with you and for you.

What a Care Team Actually Is

A good care team is one that you can lean on for preventative care, pain, diagnoses, procedures, surgery, and mental health needs. It is a group of doctors that treat existing conditions, help diagnose conditions you may not know about, and prevent other conditions from arising. A good care team listens, refers you when they don’t know the answer, and never shames you.

The Providers You Need To Know About

The good news about living in 2026 - you have options. Here is a list of doctors or specialists that might make up part (or all, do your thing) of your individual care team:

  • OB/GYN - you still need this no matter what age (also please get pap smears, they can save lives)

  • Primary Care - find one that listens to you, refers you to people when you ask, and schedules ALL types of preventative care as you age (mammograms, colonoscopies, bone density screenings, etc.)

  • Endocrinologist / Reproductive Endocrinologist- you may need this, you may not. When you need them though, you really need them (think thyroid issues, diabetes, HRT when needed, etc.)

  • Endometriosis Specialist - think someone who performs excision surgery and is an actual specialist in the field.

  • PCOS Specialist - these are harder to come by (oftentimes these are reproductive endocrinologists). If you can’t find one, ensure that your OB/GYN works with patients and treats PCOS regularly.

  • Physical Therapist

  • Pelvic Floor Physical Therapist (very different from regular physical therapist)

  • Mental Health Provider(s)

  • Registered Dietician (a nutritionist can work as well, but RDs have specialized training and are licensed)

  • Integrative Medicine Doctor - these are still MDs, but they focus on the full-body

  • Naturopath - if you want to go that route, these can be extremely helpful for some

  • Chiropractor - works for some, others not so much

  • Acupuncturist - some people hate needles and will absolutely never do this and that is ok (others say it changed their life)

  • Doula or Midwife

  • Dermatologist - hormones do weird things to our skin (and also you should be getting skin checks regularly no matter what)

  • Urologist - I’ve had to see one, it was a wild ride. They are very important if they are needed

  • Personal Trainer/Coach - someone to help you understand what exercise is best for your body, age, condition, expertise, and how to perfect form, build bone density, and build programs for you (just call me after I’m officially certified, finding this one is easy).

This list is not meant to overwhelm (nor is it completely comprehensive)- it is meant to illustrate that it takes a lot to be a functioning woman and get the care you need. This list will ebb and flow throughout your life, and you will gradually build up your team as time goes on.

What to Look For - And What to Walk Away From

This topic can (and will be) an entire piece in itself, but here are a few things to note when building your care team. Let’s start with what to walk away from:

  • If a doctor tells you that “pain is normal”- get a second opinion (there are caveats to this, but the idea still holds-most of the time you shouldn’t have to suffer)

  • If a doctor tells you that you’re “just being anxious” or to “just relax” find someone else (this happened to me- by a female doctor no less- and if I had listened I wouldn’t have found a medication that seems to be really helping me)

  • If you feel in any way dismissed, not listened to, or rushed out of a room- that doctor is not for you

  • If a doctor tries to tell you that “nothing is wrong with you” even though you’re pretty convinced something is- that doctor is also not for you

  • If you know you have a condition (i.e., endometriosis, PCOS) and you ask a doctor about it and they say “don’t worry lots of women have that, take some Tylenol” - sprint out of that doctors office

  • If you’re going in for a procedure, no matter how routine, and you know that you need medicine for pain during or after (think IUD insertion, pap smear, biopsy, transvaginal ultrasound, etc.) - you have every right to ask for it, push for it, and demand it. If they say no or that you “really don’t need it” even though you know you do- find someone else to do the procedure.

Here are some tips to build a good care team:

  • Ask, Ask, Ask: Ask your friends, coworkers, other moms in your area, or even neighbors on who they go to, who they recommend, and who they’ve had good experiences with. This is the best way to get vetted doctors and a very powerful system.

  • Use Online Resources: Many cities have Facebook groups for Endometriosis, PCOS, etc that have great doctor recommendations. Some endo patients recommend Nancy’s Nook.

  • Trust Your Gut: If you feel heard, seen, and it seems like the doctor is giving advice that works for you- stay with them.

  • Look at Universities and Research Hospitals: These are often hospitals and doctors that are leading research and using cutting edge technologies. Also, sometimes they have clinical trials going on that you can join.

  • Think About Options Outside Your City: Sometimes it is worth driving an hour (or flying) to a better doctor to get actual care. This is a very privileged option, not everyone has the luxury of doing this.

Where to Start When You Have No Idea Where to Start

Starting is hard and starting is NOT fun. Once you get momentum, it will get easier. For some, it may make sense to start with finding a good primary care, and an OB/GYN that you really like. For others, it may look like finding a specialist first, and then finding a primary care or OB/GYN doctor that your specialist likes and routinely works with. Along the way, ask them for recommendations and referrals. Build as you go, and pace your appointments so you don’t get overwhelmed.

You Do Not Have to Figure This Out Alone

Building a care team can feel overwhelming when you’re already exhausted from fighting for answers. You don’t have to figure it out alone. If any of this resonates with you and you don't know where to start, reach out. Seriously. Send me a message, reply to this email, or find me on Instagram. I am building EveryWoman for exactly this moment and I would love to help you figure out your first step. That is what I am here for.

Train through it. Recover from it. Thrive beyond it.

Madeleine

posts.bodyHtml:
For years, my body was trying to tell me something.

It started with things that were hard to explain. Pelvic pain that didn’t follow any predictable pattern. Migraines with aura so debilitating they would send me into hours of severe vomiting. A fatigue that felt like something deeper than being tired. Birth controls that didn’t work the way they were supposed to, my body reacting to hormones in ways that felt wrong but that I couldn’t quite articulate to a doctor. Symptoms that, on their own, could mean a hundred different things. Together, they added up to years of confusion, dead ends, and the slow creeping feeling that something was genuinely not right.

But I didn’t have a name for it. And without a name, it’s hard to fight for answers.

A Trip To Urgent Care

It wasn’t the diagnosis I expected.

It was the Spring of 2023 and I was (begrudgingly) rushed to urgent care with severe abdominal pain, the kind that doesn’t give you a choice about whether to go. What followed was an emergency appendectomy that very day, and multiple panicked calls to my Mom.

But here is where I got lucky, in the most unexpected way.

The surgical staff on call that day was all female. And when they went into my abdomen, they saw something. They recognized it immediately. They took photos.

When I woke up from surgery, they handed me pictures of my own insides and told me to go get it checked out. What they had found, growing across my entire abdomen, was endometriosis.

I remember staring at those photos, the anesthesia drugs still swirling in my system, and feeling the hot tears starting to roll down my cheeks.

“Just Take Some Tylenol”

(This header is a personal pet peeve of mine, you’ll see why.)

I went back to my OB/GYN not long after surgery frightened and looking for answers. She was the doctor I had trusted, the one I had been seeing for a few years. I sat in her office with those photos in my hand and told her what the surgical team had found.

Her response was something close to a shrug.

Tons of women have endometriosis, she told me. Take some Tylenol.

I want to pause here, because I know some of you reading this have heard something almost exactly like that. Maybe not those words, but that sentiment. That dismissal dressed up as reassurance. That sense of a door closing before you even got to ask your real questions.

I left that appointment feeling more lost than when I walked in. Was I actually just fine? Why did those surgeons make this sound like such a big deal? A ton of women have this?

Getting A Second Opinion

Around that time, a woman who I worked with stepped in.

After I told her about the surgeons finding endometriosis, she insisted I go and see a specialist. Not a general OB/GYN. A specialist. She passed on the name of her doctor in San Diego, and a month later I was sitting in a new office, holding those same photos, waiting.

What that doctor told me stopped me cold.

My endometriosis was severe. It had been spreading across my abdomen, making its way towards my lungs and liver. I needed an excision surgery, and I needed it soon, before it spread further. This was not a Tylenol situation. This had never been a Tylenol situation. After the appointment, I went to the parking garage and called my Mom, sobbing and shocked at how severe this was without me knowing.

I think about what might have happened if that woman hadn’t intervened. If I had taken my first OB/GYN’s advice and just managed the symptoms. How much further it would have spread, the fertility I almost certainly would’ve lost. How much longer I would have gone without understanding what was happening inside my own body.

The Excision Surgery

I went in for excision surgery in September of 2023.

Two days later I was back in the emergency room, this time with a severe kidney infection. I was vomiting and shaking so badly I couldn’t move. In 2023 alone, I had seven bacterial infections. Seven. My body had been through surgery, through crisis, through recovery, and it kept getting hit.

That year was so hard. That’s it. It was just hard. And it sucked. Thank you for reading my very elegant thoughts on that experience.

My body never really seemed to recover fully. It felt like the disease, once somewhat silent and manageable, became very loud and chaotic within a matter of months.

Life After

After the diagnosis and surgery, my life became a series of appointments, doctors, urgent care, and pain.

I developed fatigue that was so debilitating, no amount of sleep would help. I couldn’t make it through the day without taking naps and resting constantly. I developed “crash outs” where after simply walking the dog around the block, I’d have to lay for days to recover. My stomach began swelling at random times so no pants would fit (this is called endo belly I would come to find out). I was put on two different types of birth controls to try to stop endometriosis regrowth and stop symptoms, both of which caused my migraines to get much worse and make my body feel completely off.

I began gaining weight even though I was eating healthy and exercising as much as I possibly could (if you know me, you know I’m a big swimmer and I love lifting weights).

I was seeing specialists, and doctors, and getting constant blood draws. I was begging doctors to help me and help with these symptoms. I was being told I did have PCOS, then that I didn’t (jury is still out on that I guess). I was making all the lifestyle shifts the experts said to make. I was taking fistfuls of supplements every day. Nothing was working. I was begging for them to listen and to understand that I was SO TIRED. LIKE ALL THE TIME.

The Mayo Clinic

It was now 2025 and I felt so sick. I felt so tired. I had been to my surgeon, an endocrinologist, three GPs, an OBGYN, another endometriosis doctor, an acupuncturist, a pelvic floor PT (which by the way was amazing and probably the only doctor I liked going to), a naturopath, a dietician, a trainer, three therapists, and more.

After calling my Dad one day, he suggested looking into the Mayo Clinic. I applied online and (much to my shock) got accepted. My Mom met me at the Phoenix campus, and the doctor listened and agreed that the fatigue was not normal. He referred me to endocrinology, and after a full day of tests, they found nothing alarming in my bloodwork or in all of the extra tests they ran. They did find more endometriosis in a pelvic MRI (which we all knew and expected to be back, we just didn’t know how much would be there). From there, they sent me to the integrative medicine department.

After spending over an hour talking about what felt like my entire life and entire medical history, the doctor diagnosed me with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME). We’re not sure if endometriosis caused it, if another virus caused it (hello mono), or how endometriosis and CFS are related (my gut says they are INCREDIBLY related, more on that later). We talked through more things I could do to help my body, and some medication options to actually help me with the debilitating fatigue. I started Low-Dose Naltrexone (LDN), and really worked (and still work) with her on areas that can serve me.

I don’t feel perfect, but I feel a little better with the LDN and some of this doctor’s advice. I started working with a world renowned coach, Loretta Hogg, to dive more into weight lifting and using it as a way to help with energy and muscle mass. I actively work on “pacing” (which is very hard for me to do given my personality). Most of all, I recognize that this is a lifelong disease that will more than likely ebb and flow (which is also very hard for me to do given my personality). And ok, I’ll admit that I’m still actively working on this “acceptance” piece.

Why EveryWoman

You just spent an inordinate amount of time reading about the last three years of my life- thank you for this. Not everything I post on here will be a sob story, most of it will be actionable, and helpful for women at all stages of their lives. I’ve spent three years entirely focused and dedicated to women’s health: learning, studying, reading books and articles, talking to doctors, training intensively with many trainers and women’s PTs, and trying everything under the sun. I think it might be time do something with that and give back a little bit.

I am currently training to become a certified women's coach because I want to do for other women what the women in my life did for me. Point them toward answers. Help them build care teams that actually see them. Show them that movement and strength training can be part of healing, not separate from it.

EveryWoman is for every woman who has ever had a symptom dismissed. Who has been handed a Tylenol and sent home. Who has felt like the medical system, the fitness world, and every generic wellness space wasn’t built with her body in mind. Essentially, EveryWoman is something I just really wish I had access to three years ago.

Whether you are navigating endometriosis, PCOS, perimenopause, menopause, or the pre and postpartum journey, you deserve support that sees the whole picture. You deserve a care team that fights for you. You deserve to feel strong in your body, whatever stage it is in.

That is what I am building here. And I’m launching it during Endometriosis Awareness Month (no better time!).

I am so glad you found it.

Train through it. Recover from it. Thrive beyond it.

-Madeleine

(P.S. A public thank you to my Mom who has been at every surgery and appointment, and who always takes a call from me, no matter how upset I am or how much I cry. Without you, this would not be a thing. I love you.)
